small_guidance:
- The softmax kernel is likely the bottleneck for N=8192: try a single-pass online softmax (track running max + sum) to halve the global memory traffic from 3 reads to 2; also sweep BLOCK_N in {1024, 2048, 4096, 8192} with num_warps in {8, 16}, num_stages=2.
- Add a GROUP_M block-swizzle (GROUP_M=8) to gemm_bn_scale_kernel to improve L2 reuse on the 1024×8192 output, and add larger autotune configs (e.g. BLOCK_M=128/BLOCK_N=256/BLOCK_K=64, num_warps=8, num_stages=4) since K=8192 has lots of room to overlap.
- Pre-transpose W once at init to (K, N) contiguous so the inner K-loop loads B with stride 1 along K (currently B is loaded with stride_wk on the inner axis), removing strided loads in the hot loop.
large_guidance:
- Fuse GEMM + BN-scale + softmax into a single persistent kernel: one program per row tile that computes a full row of N=8192 outputs, then performs the row-wise max/sum/normalize in registers/SMEM before storing — this eliminates the intermediate `out` tensor (32 MB) write+read entirely.
- If a fused single-kernel is too large, at minimum fuse the row-max into the GEMM epilogue (compute partial max per N-tile, atomically combine, then a small second kernel does sum-exp + normalize), turning a 3-pass softmax into a 2-pass scheme with one fewer global read of the GEMM output.
- Consider splitK or persistent-CTA GEMM with M=1024, N=8192, K=8192 (very square): a persistent kernel with GROUP_M swizzle and 128×256×64 tiles tends to outperform the naive grid on Ada; combine with TF32 `tl.dot(..., allow_tf32=True)` for further speedup if accuracy permits.
